Hawaiian foods.Poke: Meaning 'to slice' in Hawaiian, poke was once fishermen's seasoned scraps of reef fish and is now a mainland bowl craze.
Hawaiian foods.Spam musubi: A slice of grilled Spam on rice, wrapped in nori; Hawaiians eat more Spam per person than any other US state.
Hawaiian foods.Loco moco: A hamburger patty over rice, topped with a fried egg and gravy; it was reportedly invented in Hilo in the 1940s.
Hawaiian foods.Kalua pig: Pork slow-cooked in an underground oven called an imu, wrapped in banana or ti leaves, is the centerpiece of a luau.
Hawaiian foods.Poi: Mashed taro root, once the staple food of Hawaii, is a sticky purple paste that ferments slightly and turns tangy.
Hawaiian foods.Shave ice: Finely shaved ice soaked in flavored syrups, often over ice cream and azuki beans, was influenced by Japanese immigrants.
Hawaiian foods.Malasadas: Portuguese immigrants brought these sugar-coated, hole-less doughnuts to Hawaii's plantations, and they're now a local favorite.
Hawaiian foods.Lomi lomi salmon: Diced salted salmon, tomato and onion 'massaged' together, the name means to rub; the salmon came with whalers and sailors.
Hawaiian foods.Haupia: A firm coconut milk pudding, cut in squares, is a luau dessert thickened traditionally with arrowroot or pia.
Hawaiian foods.Huli huli chicken: 'Huli' means 'turn' in Hawaiian, as in rotating the chickens on a rotisserie with a sweet teriyaki-like glaze.
Hawaiian foods.Ceviche: Raw fish in citrus, a close cousin of poke, but it's Peruvian, not Hawaiian.
Hawaiian foods.Pad thai: The Thai noodle dish is a popular export, but has no place in Hawaiian tradition.
Hawaiian foods.Jerk chicken: Jamaica's spicy grilled chicken is Caribbean, though Hawaii's huli huli chicken is a sweeter cousin in spirit.
Hawaiian foods.Gumbo: Louisiana's thick stew has no part in Hawaiian cuisine.
Hawaiian foods.Pupusa: This stuffed corn tortilla is the Salvadoran national dish, not a Hawaiian food.
Hawaiian foods.Feijoada: Brazil's black bean stew is South American.
Hawaiian foods.Tacos al pastor: Mexican pork tacos shaved from a spit, inspired by Lebanese shawarma brought by immigrants; not Hawaiian.
Hawaiian foods.Clam chowder: A New England creamy soup from the northeastern US, not Hawaiian.
Hawaiian foods.Bibimbap: A Korean mixed rice bowl, though Hawaii's large Korean community has made Korean-style barbecue popular there, bibimbap itself isn't Hawaiian.
Hawaiian foods.Pierogi: Polish stuffed dumplings, a trap only if you think of Hawaii's melting pot; they're Eastern European.
Hawaiian foods.Jambalaya: A spiced rice dish of Louisiana Creole and Cajun cooking, not Hawaiian.
Hawaiian foods.Poutine: Quebec's fries, curds and gravy, a Canadian dish.
Hawaiian foods.Tteokbokki: Spicy Korean rice cakes in red chili sauce are a Korean street food, not Hawaiian.
Hawaiian foods.Haggis: Scotland's sheep-offal pudding has nothing to do with Hawaii.

Marsupials.Kangaroo: Marsupials carry their young in pouches. A newborn kangaroo is about the size of a jellybean when it crawls into the pouch.
Marsupials.Koala: A marsupial, not a bear. Its pouch opens backwards, and it sleeps up to around 20 hours a day on a low-energy eucalyptus diet.
Marsupials.Wombat: A marsupial whose backward-facing pouch keeps dirt out when it digs. It is famous for producing cube-shaped droppings.
Marsupials.Opossum: North America's only marsupial. Mothers carry a dozen or more babies, and they famously play dead when threatened.
Marsupials.Wallaby: A smaller relative of the kangaroo. Wallabies are marsupials, and the young stay in the pouch for several months.
Marsupials.Tasmanian devil: A carnivorous marsupial with one of the strongest bites for its size. It lives wild only on the island of Tasmania.
Marsupials.Sugar glider: A small marsupial that glides between trees on skin flaps stretched between its wrists and ankles, for 45 metres or more.
Marsupials.Bandicoot: A small Australasian marsupial with a pouch that opens backwards. It has a long snout for digging up insects.
Marsupials.Quokka: A small marsupial from Western Australia, often called the world's happiest animal for its seemingly smiling face.
Marsupials.Numbat: A termite-eating marsupial from Western Australia with a striped back. Uniquely among marsupials, it is active mainly in daytime.
Marsupials.Bilby: A long-eared desert marsupial from Australia. It burrows, and in Australia a chocolate bilby is an Easter alternative to the bunny.
Marsupials.Platypus: A trap: it is an Australian mammal, but it lays eggs. It is a monotreme, not a marsupial, and has no pouch.
Marsupials.Echidna: Another Australian egg-layer. As a monotreme, it is not a marsupial, though the baby does develop in a temporary pouch.
Marsupials.Dingo: Australia's wild dog is a placental mammal. It arrived with humans thousands of years ago and has no pouch.
Marsupials.Raccoon: A placental mammal from North America known for its dexterous front paws. It is often mistaken for a marsupial, but is not.
Marsupials.Squirrel: A placental rodent, like most mammals. Squirrels bury many nuts and forget some, helping to plant forests.
Marsupials.Sloth: A slow-moving placental mammal from Central and South America. It has no pouch and climbs down trees only about once a week.
Marsupials.Lemur: A primate from Madagascar. Lemurs are placental mammals, found nowhere wild except on that island and nearby islands.
Marsupials.Hamster: A rodent, so a placental mammal. Hamsters stuff food into stretchy cheek pouches, which are not the same as marsupial pouches.
Marsupials.Meerkat: A placental mammal from southern Africa. These social mongooses take turns acting as sentries for the group.
Marsupials.Armadillo: Another placental mammal, with bony plates. Nine-banded armadillos always give birth to identical quadruplets.
Marsupials.Flying fox: A big fruit bat, so a placental mammal. Some have wingspans of well over a metre, and no pouch at all.
Marsupials.Emu: A bird, not a marsupial, though it is famously Australian. The emu appears alongside the kangaroo on Australia's coat of arms.
Marsupials.Kookaburra: A kingfisher, so a bird. Its loud call sounds like laughter, and it's a big Australian icon, but it is not a marsupial.

Types of storm.Hurricane: Hurricanes are fed by warm ocean water and can release energy comparable to many times the world's electricity use, and they're named in rotating lists.
Types of storm.Tornado: Tornadoes are rotating columns of air with winds that can exceed 400 km/h in the strongest, and most form in the United States.
Types of storm.Blizzard: A blizzard is not just heavy snow, but strong winds of about 56 km/h plus low visibility lasting several hours.
Types of storm.Typhoon: Typhoon is the name for a hurricane-type storm in the northwest Pacific, and Pacific storms can be the largest on Earth.
Types of storm.Cyclone: Cyclones are the same kind of storm as hurricanes and typhoons, and the name is used in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.
Types of storm.Thunderstorm: A thunderstorm produces lightning, and at any moment there are roughly 2,000 of them going on around the planet.
Types of storm.Sandstorm: Sandstorms can lift desert dust into walls up to a kilometer high, and Saharan dust fertilizes the Amazon.
Types of storm.Hailstorm: Hailstorms can drop ice balls as large as softballs, and the biggest recorded stone in the US weighed nearly a kilo.
Types of storm.Derecho: A derecho is a long-lived windstorm that sweeps across a wide area in a line of thunderstorms, and it can match hurricane-force winds.
Types of storm.Nor'easter: A nor'easter is a strong coastal storm in the northeastern US named for its winds off the northeast, and it can bring heavy snow.
Types of storm.Ice storm: An ice storm coats everything with freezing rain, and just a centimeter of ice can bring down power lines.
Types of storm.Drizzle: Drizzle is very light rain with tiny droplets, so it's not a storm.
Types of storm.Fog: Fog is a cloud at ground level, and calm and fine, so it isn't stormy.
Types of storm.Dew: Dew forms when surfaces cool enough to turn water vapor into droplets, and is a quiet, daily event.
Types of storm.Frost: Frost is ice crystals that form on cold surfaces, and not itself a storm.
Types of storm.Rainbow: A rainbow forms when sunlight bends and reflects in raindrops, and appears after storms, not as one.
Types of storm.Breeze: A breeze is just a gentle wind, nowhere near storm strength.
Types of storm.Drought: A drought is a long period without rain, the opposite of a storm, and it can last for years.
Types of storm.Mist: A mist is a thin fog of tiny droplets, much gentler than a storm.
Types of storm.Haze: A haze is fine particles of dust or smoke reducing visibility, not a storm.
Types of storm.Earthquake: An earthquake is a shaking of the ground, so it's a geological event, not weather.
Types of storm.Tsunami: A tsunami is a series of giant waves usually caused by undersea earthquakes, not by weather.
Types of storm.Avalanche: An avalanche is a slide of snow down a slope, often triggered by weather but not itself a storm.
Types of storm.Heatwave: A heatwave is a long period of abnormally hot weather, a danger, but not a storm.

Waterfalls.Niagara Falls: It is not tall, but its volume is huge. It straddles the US-Canada border and has eroded several kilometers upstream since the Ice Age.
Waterfalls.Victoria Falls: Locals call it Mosi-oa-Tunya, the smoke that thunders, and its spray can be seen from kilometers away. It lies between Zambia and Zimbabwe.
Waterfalls.Angel Falls: At 979 m, Venezuela's Angel Falls is the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall, named for pilot Jimmie Angel.
Waterfalls.Iguazu Falls: On the Argentina-Brazil border, it has about 275 separate drops, the biggest of which is the Devil's Throat.
Waterfalls.Yosemite Falls: California's falls are among the tallest in North America, dropping about 740 m in three stages.
Waterfalls.Gullfoss: Iceland's Golden Falls plunges in two stages into a canyon, and it is a highlight of the Golden Circle.
Waterfalls.Rhine Falls: The most powerful waterfall on the plains of Europe lies near Schaffhausen in Switzerland.
Waterfalls.Kaieteur Falls: Guyana's falls drop about 226 m in a single leap, much taller than Niagara, deep in the rainforest.
Waterfalls.Sutherland Falls: Over 580 m high, New Zealand's falls lie along the famous Milford Track.
Waterfalls.Multnomah Falls: Oregon's falls drop about 189 m and are among the most visited natural attractions in the Pacific Northwest.
Waterfalls.Tugela Falls: South Africa's Drakensberg falls plunge nearly 950 m in five drops, making it one of the tallest in the world.
Waterfalls.Grand Canyon: The Colorado River carved this giant gorge, but it is a canyon rather than a waterfall.
Waterfalls.Old Faithful: Yellowstone's geyser erupts about every 90 minutes, which is water shooting up rather than falling.
Waterfalls.Blue Lagoon: Iceland's milky blue pool is a man-made lake fed by geothermal power plant runoff, not a waterfall.
Waterfalls.Great Barrier Reef: It is the largest coral reef system in the world, visible from space, but it has no waterfall.
Waterfalls.Dead Sea: This salt lake has no outlet, so it cannot have a waterfall; it is so salty that swimmers float.
Waterfalls.Ha Long Bay: Vietnam's bay is dotted with about 1,600 limestone islands, rather than waterfalls.
Waterfalls.Uluru: Australia's giant sandstone monolith has no permanent waterfall, but briefly shows waterfalls after heavy rain.
Waterfalls.Cliffs of Moher: Ireland's sea cliffs rise up to 214 m above the Atlantic, with no waterfall.
Waterfalls.Giant's Causeway: Northern Ireland's coast has basalt columns, and none of them is a waterfall.
Waterfalls.Pamukkale: A trap. Turkey's white travertine terraces look like frozen waterfalls, but they are mineral deposits.
Waterfalls.Mount Fuji: Japan's volcano is a peak, not a waterfall, but it is surrounded by lakes.
Waterfalls.Strokkur: Iceland's geyser erupts every 5 to 10 minutes, shooting water upward, not down.
Waterfalls.Monument Valley: The sandstone buttes in the Navajo Nation were made famous by John Ford's westerns.

Sights in San Francisco.Golden Gate Bridge: Despite its name, the bridge is painted International Orange, a color chosen so it stands out in San Francisco's fog.
Sights in San Francisco.Alcatraz: The island prison closed in 1963, and later became a national park drawing over a million visitors a year.
Sights in San Francisco.Lombard Street: Its famous hairpin turns, eight in one block, were added in the 1920s to make the steep hill drivable.
Sights in San Francisco.Fisherman's Wharf: Sea lions famously crowd the floating docks nearby, and the wharf is known for Dungeness crab and sourdough bread bowls.
Sights in San Francisco.Haight-Ashbury: This neighborhood was the center of the 1967 Summer of Love, when about 100,000 young people flocked to San Francisco.
Sights in San Francisco.Coit Tower: The 210-foot tower atop Telegraph Hill was funded by a bequest from Lillie Coit, and it holds Depression-era murals inside.
Sights in San Francisco.Pier 39: A wooden pier turned shopping center, famous for the sea lions that moved onto its docks after the 1989 earthquake.
Sights in San Francisco.Painted Ladies: These colorful Victorian houses on Alamo Square are best known from the opening credits of the sitcom Full House.
Sights in San Francisco.Twin Peaks: Two hills near the city's center offer a panoramic view, and the Spanish once called them El Pecho de la Chola, the Breasts of the Maiden.
Sights in San Francisco.Presidio: This former military post, run by the Army for over 200 years, is now a huge park with the bridge's southern end beside it.
Sights in San Francisco.Hollywood Sign: It is in Los Angeles, and originally read Hollywoodland as a real estate ad, losing its last four letters later.
Sights in San Francisco.Venice Beach: Los Angeles's boardwalk, famous for Muscle Beach and skaters, was inspired by Venice, Italy, with canals still lining nearby streets.
Sights in San Francisco.Santa Monica Pier: This Los Angeles-area landmark marks the end of Route 66 in popular lore and has a solar-powered Ferris wheel.
Sights in San Francisco.Disneyland: It is in Anaheim, Southern California, and opened in 1955 as the only theme park Walt Disney personally oversaw.
Sights in San Francisco.Space Needle: A trap for the Bay Area: this landmark belongs to Seattle, built for the 1962 World's Fair.
Sights in San Francisco.Pike Place Market: This Seattle market, open since 1907, is known for fish tossing and the first Starbucks store, not San Francisco.
Sights in San Francisco.Napa Valley: The wine region is about an hour's drive north of San Francisco, so it is nearby but not in the city.
Sights in San Francisco.Yosemite: Yosemite National Park is a few hours' drive east of the city, home to El Capitan and Half Dome.
Sights in San Francisco.Hearst Castle: Newspaper tycoon William Randolph Hearst built this lavish estate on the central coast, about 200 miles south of San Francisco.
Sights in San Francisco.Big Sur: This rugged stretch of coastline south of Monterey is famously beautiful, and Highway 1 there has landslide closures often.
Sights in San Francisco.Griffith Observatory: It stands on a Los Angeles hillside, and shows up in the film Rebel Without a Cause, so it is far from San Francisco.
Sights in San Francisco.Muir Woods: Muir Woods, in Marin County just across the Golden Gate Bridge, protects old-growth coast redwoods, so it is near but outside the city.
Sights in San Francisco.Silicon Valley: Tech's heartland lies south of San Francisco around San Jose, and its name came from the silicon in computer chips.
Sights in San Francisco.Lake Tahoe: About a four-hour drive east in the Sierra Nevada, North America's largest alpine lake is famously clear and cold.

SI units.Meter: The meter is now defined by the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second; it began as a ten-millionth of the pole-to-equator distance.
SI units.Kilogram: Since 2019 the kilogram has been defined via the Planck constant, retiring the platinum-iridium cylinder.
SI units.Second: The second is defined by 9,192,631,770 vibrations of the cesium-133 atom.
SI units.Ampere: The ampere measures electric current and since 2019 is defined by fixing the charge of the electron.
SI units.Kelvin: The kelvin is the SI unit of temperature, where 0 K is absolute zero, and there's no degree sign.
SI units.Mole: A mole is about 6.022 times 10 to the 23rd particles, Avogadro's number.
SI units.Candela: The candela measures luminous intensity and is the least familiar base unit; the name comes from candle.
SI units.Newton: A newton is roughly the weight of a small apple, and is the force that accelerates 1 kg at 1 m/s squared.
SI units.Joule: The joule is named for James Joule, a brewer's son who measured heat's mechanical equivalent.
SI units.Watt: James Watt also coined horsepower to sell his steam engines, and a watt is one joule per second.
SI units.Volt: The volt is named for Alessandro Volta, who invented the battery in 1800.
SI units.Ohm: The ohm honors Georg Ohm, whose law of resistance was first poorly received.
SI units.Pascal: The pascal is tiny; atmospheric pressure is about 101,000 pascals.
SI units.Hertz: The hertz honors Heinrich Hertz, who proved radio waves exist; one hertz is one cycle per second.
SI units.Coulomb: A coulomb is about 6.24 quintillion electron charges.
SI units.Mile: The mile is an imperial unit, not part of SI.
SI units.Pound: The pound is imperial, though it's now legally defined by the kilogram.
SI units.Foot: The foot is imperial, and exactly 0.3048 meters since 1959.
SI units.Inch: The inch is exactly 2.54 centimeters, but not an SI unit.
SI units.Calorie: The calorie is a metric energy unit but not SI; the joule is.
SI units.Horsepower: Horsepower was coined by James Watt and isn't SI.
SI units.Gallon: The gallon differs between the US and the UK and isn't SI.
SI units.Ounce: The ounce comes from Latin for a twelfth and is not SI.
SI units.Fahrenheit: A trap: Fahrenheit is a temperature scale used in the US; the SI unit for temperature is the kelvin.

Movie characters you wouldn't invite to.Kermit the Frog: The laid-back Muppet host is kind and friendly, and always trying to keep his chaotic friends in order.
Movie characters you wouldn't invite to.Mrs. Doubtfire: Robin Williams's comic nanny is a warm presence, though the dinner might include a scene with a mask of her own face.
Movie characters you wouldn't invite to.Hermione: Hermione is a brilliant, kind witch who would help with the dishes, using magic, and bring spell tips.
Movie characters you wouldn't invite to.Woody: The loyal cowboy toy always looks after his friends, which makes him a welcoming guest and not a villain.

String instruments.Violin: Antonio Stradivari built violins in the early 1700s that still sell for millions, and scientists haven't fully explained their sound.
String instruments.Viola: Slightly larger and lower than a violin, it reads the alto clef, a notation that few other instruments use.
String instruments.Cello: Its name is short for violoncello, meaning 'little big violone', and the instrument is played seated, held between the knees.
String instruments.Double bass: The largest bowed string instrument is standard in orchestras and jazz bands, and is tuned in fourths like a bass guitar.
String instruments.Harp: A concert harp has 47 strings and seven pedals, which change the pitch of each note.
String instruments.Guitar: The modern guitar descends from older instruments such as the Spanish vihuela, and the classical form was settled in the 1800s.
String instruments.Banjo: It came to America from West Africa, brought by enslaved people, before it became a signature sound of bluegrass.
String instruments.Mandolin: Its strings are in pairs tuned like a violin's, so players use rapid picking, a tremolo, to hold a note.
String instruments.Ukulele: Its Hawaiian name is often translated 'jumping flea', and it was adapted from small Portuguese guitars brought to Hawaii in the 1870s.
String instruments.Sitar: The Indian instrument became known in the West thanks to Ravi Shankar, who taught George Harrison, who used it on Norwegian Wood.
String instruments.Lute: A pear-shaped, plucked instrument that was Europe's favorite in the Renaissance, and its name gave 'luthier' to all string-instrument makers.
String instruments.Zither: Its strings are stretched over a flat sound box, and the zither's twangy theme in 1949's The Third Man became a hit.
String instruments.Flute: A woodwind: the player blows across a hole, so air, not a string, makes the sound. Archaeologists have found flutes about 40,000 years old.
String instruments.Oboe: A double-reed woodwind, and the instrument whose 'A' note the whole orchestra tunes to before a concert.
String instruments.Trumpet: A brass instrument: the player's buzzing lips create the sound, with no strings, and Tutankhamun's tomb held two trumpets.
String instruments.Xylophone: A percussion instrument of tuned wooden bars struck by mallets, so it makes sound without strings.
String instruments.Clarinet: A single-reed woodwind, and Mozart's Clarinet Concerto is one of the best known pieces for it. There are no strings to pluck.
String instruments.Tuba: The largest brass instrument, with the lowest voice, takes about 18 feet of tubing, and the sound comes from the lips and not from strings.
String instruments.Harmonica: A free-reed wind instrument. Players blow and draw air across tiny metal reeds, so it has no strings.
String instruments.Accordion: Bellows push air across reeds, making it a free-reed instrument, though it has a keyboard-like layout, but no strings.
String instruments.Bagpipes: They sound by air from a bag across reeds, and are not strung. A drone is a constant held note.
String instruments.Triangle: A bent steel bar struck with a beater is percussion, which is easily overlooked but loud enough to cut through an orchestra.
String instruments.Kazoo: It buzzes a membrane when you hum into it, and is called a membranophone, not a stringed instrument.
String instruments.Ocarina: A small ceramic wind instrument, made famous to gamers by The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and has no strings.

Music genres born in the USA.Jazz: Born in New Orleans in the early 1900s, from blues, ragtime and brass band music.
Music genres born in the USA.Blues: Rooted in the Mississippi Delta, with roots in spirituals and work songs.
Music genres born in the USA.Rock and roll: Disc jockey Alan Freed popularised the term in the early 1950s. Chuck Berry and Elvis made it a global sound.
Music genres born in the USA.Hip hop: Many trace its birth to a Bronx party in August 1973, where DJ Kool Herc extended the breaks with two turntables.
Music genres born in the USA.Country: The 1927 Bristol Sessions in Tennessee are often called its big bang, as they recorded Jimmie Rodgers and the Carter Family.
Music genres born in the USA.Bluegrass: Named after Bill Monroe's Blue Grass Boys, and named for Kentucky, the Bluegrass State.
Music genres born in the USA.Gospel: Thomas A. Dorsey, a bluesman turned church composer, is called its father, and he wrote Take My Hand, Precious Lord.
Music genres born in the USA.Funk: James Brown pushed it by putting the stress on the first beat of the bar, which he called the one.
Music genres born in the USA.Soul: Aretha Franklin and Motown made it famous, and Ray Charles had fused gospel with R&B earlier.
Music genres born in the USA.Grunge: Seattle's Sub Pop label pushed it in the late 1980s, and Nirvana's Nevermind made it global in 1991.
Music genres born in the USA.House: It takes its name from the Warehouse club in Chicago, where DJ Frankie Knuckles played in the early 1980s.
Music genres born in the USA.Techno: Born in Detroit in the mid-1980s, shaped by the Belleville Three. Techno is Detroit's gift to electronic music.
Music genres born in the USA.Swing: Benny Goodman, the King of Swing, brought big-band swing to mass audiences in the 1930s.
Music genres born in the USA.Reggae: Born in Jamaica in the late 1960s, with Toots and the Maytals' song Do the Reggay giving it its name.
Music genres born in the USA.Ska: A Jamaican style from the 1950s, and ancestor of rocksteady and reggae, with an offbeat guitar chop.
Music genres born in the USA.Samba: Brazil's carnival music, and the soundtrack of Rio's samba schools.
Music genres born in the USA.Flamenco: Born in Andalusia, Spain, and listed by UNESCO as intangible heritage in 2010.
Music genres born in the USA.K-pop: South Korea's pop machine took off in the 1990s, with Seo Taiji and Boys' 1992 debut a milestone.
Music genres born in the USA.Bossa nova: Brazilian, and it blends samba and jazz. A trap, because American jazz musicians loved it and made it big in the US.
Music genres born in the USA.Calypso: Trinidad's music. A 1956 craze in the US is a trap, since Harry Belafonte's calypso albums made it big there.
Music genres born in the USA.Fado: Portugal's mournful music of longing, centred on the Portuguese word saudade.
Music genres born in the USA.Tango: Born in Buenos Aires and Montevideo in the 1880s, so it is the Rio de la Plata, not the USA.
Music genres born in the USA.Britpop: 1990s British guitar pop, and the 1995 Blur versus Oasis chart battle was its peak.
Music genres born in the USA.Mariachi: Mexico's, from Jalisco, and UNESCO listed mariachi as intangible heritage in 2011.

Things that tick.Clock: The tick is the escapement releasing the gear one tooth at a time, and it's the sound of time being counted out.
Things that tick.Watch: A mechanical watch typically beats five to ten times a second, which is why it sounds smooth up close.
Things that tick.Time bomb: The ticking time bomb is a film staple, though real timers often use silent electronics.
Things that tick.Metronome: Mälzel patented the metronome in 1815, and Beethoven was an early adopter of its tempo numbers.
Things that tick.Stopwatch: A stopwatch has ticked for sports since the 1800s, though timing to a hundredth of a second came much later.
Things that tick.Geiger counter: The Geiger counter clicks for each radiation event, a sound named after physicist Hans Geiger.
Things that tick.Kitchen timer: A wind-up kitchen timer ticks as a spring unwinds, and rings when it ends.
Things that tick.Grandfather clock: The name 'grandfather clock' came from an 1876 song, My Grandfather's Clock, rather than any clockmaker.
Things that tick.Turn signal: The click is a relay mimicking old flashers; some electric cars add a fake sound for the driver.
Things that tick.Hourglass: An hourglass is silent; sand falls grain by grain without any ticking.
Things that tick.Sundial: A sundial uses a moving shadow to tell time, and it doesn't tick at all.
Things that tick.Calendar: A calendar tracks days silently, and it has no moving parts to make a tick.
Things that tick.Candle: A candle burns quietly, with only an occasional crackle or sputter when damp.
Things that tick.Lighthouse: A lighthouse flashes light on a rotating pattern instead of ticking, so each lighthouse has its own signature.
Things that tick.Kettle: A kettle whistles or clicks off, but it doesn't tick off seconds.
Things that tick.Fridge: A fridge hums and clicks as the compressor switches on, but it doesn't keep time.
Things that tick.Doorbell: A doorbell dings or chimes rather than ticks, even the old mechanical kind.
Things that tick.Cow: Cows moo, and the only ticks nearby are parasites on the animal itself.
Things that tick.Kazoo: The kazoo buzzes when you hum into it, with a membrane that vibrates and no ticking.
Things that tick.Piano: A piano strikes strings with felt hammers, giving notes that ring and fade rather than tick.
Things that tick.Trumpet: A trumpet blares through vibrating lips and a brass tube, and not with a regular tick.
Things that tick.Snowflake: Snowflakes fall without making a sound, and no two are quite the same.
Things that tick.Pillow: A pillow is soft and silent, with nothing in it to make a tick.
Things that tick.Digital clock: A digital clock has no moving parts, so it keeps time without a tick, unlike its mechanical cousins.

Swedish music acts.ABBA: ABBA won Eurovision in 1974 with Waterloo, and the group's name comes from the first letters of its four members.
Swedish music acts.Roxette: Roxette, led by Per Gessle and Marie Fredriksson, recorded It Must Have Been Love for the film Pretty Woman.
Swedish music acts.Avicii: Avicii, real name Tim Bergling, scored a worldwide hit with Wake Me Up, which mixed folk with dance music.
Swedish music acts.Robyn: Robyn's Dancing on My Own is one of pop's great sad-yet-danceable songs, and she writes and produces much of her work.
Swedish music acts.Ace of Base: Ace of Base, from Gothenburg, had a huge worldwide hit with The Sign, which topped the US charts in 1994.
Swedish music acts.Loreen: Loreen won Eurovision in 2012 with Euphoria and again in 2023 with Tattoo, making her the first woman to win twice.
Swedish music acts.Zara Larsson: Zara Larsson won Sweden's Talang contest at age ten, and she became a pop star in her late teens.
Swedish music acts.The Cardigans: The Cardigans, from Jönköping, had Lovefool, which shot to fame after it appeared in the film Romeo + Juliet.
Swedish music acts.Swedish House Mafia: Swedish House Mafia is Axwell, Steve Angello and Sebastian Ingrosso, and they sold out huge arenas in the 2010s.
Swedish music acts.Tove Lo: Tove Lo broke through with Habits (Stay High), a candid song about coping with a breakup.
Swedish music acts.Ghost: Ghost is a masked Swedish metal band, fronted by a series of characters called Papa Emeritus, mixing horror with melodies.
Swedish music acts.a-ha: a-ha is Norwegian, from Oslo, and they sang the Bond theme The Living Daylights.
Swedish music acts.Björk: Björk is Icelandic, from Reykjavik, and she began her career as a child singer.
Swedish music acts.Kygo: Kygo is Norwegian, from Bergen, known for tropical house.
Swedish music acts.Aqua: Aqua is Danish, and their Barbie Girl got Mattel to sue them in the late 1990s.
Swedish music acts.Alan Walker: Alan Walker was born in England but raised in Norway, so he's often assumed to be Swedish.
Swedish music acts.Sigur Rós: Sigur Rós is Icelandic, and sings partly in an invented language called Hopelandic.
Swedish music acts.Daft Punk: Daft Punk is French, from Paris, and formed in the early 1990s.
Swedish music acts.Lukas Graham: Lukas Graham is Danish, from Copenhagen, and 7 Years was a 2015 hit.
Swedish music acts.Kraftwerk: Kraftwerk is German, from Düsseldorf, and pioneered electronic pop in the 1970s.
Swedish music acts.Rammstein: Rammstein is German, and they sing mostly in German, with a spectacular live show full of fire.
Swedish music acts.Scorpions: Scorpions are German, from Hanover, and their Wind of Change became an anthem of the fall of the Berlin Wall.
Swedish music acts.The Rasmus: The Rasmus is Finnish, from Helsinki, and their 2003 hit In the Shadows was a big success.
Swedish music acts.Nightwish: Nightwish is Finnish, from Kitee, and known for operatic symphonic metal.

Things an angler uses.Rod: Early rods were made of bamboo cane, and today most are carbon fiber, which is lighter and stronger.
Things an angler uses.Reel: It stores the line and winds in the fish; fly reels often just hold line, not help in fighting.
Things an angler uses.Hook: Bone fishhooks have been found that are tens of thousands of years old.
Things an angler uses.Bait: Worms, minnows and even bread work, and the best choice depends on what the fish are eating.
Things an angler uses.Lure: Shiny spoons, plugs and spinners imitate prey and trigger a predator's strike.
Things an angler uses.Bobber: It floats on the surface, and when it bobs down, it signals a bite.
Things an angler uses.Sinker: The weight sinks the bait, and lead is restricted in some places because it poisons waterbirds.
Things an angler uses.Tackle box: Anglers store hooks, lures and line here, and these compartments can be remarkably elaborate.
Things an angler uses.Landing net: It helps lift a fish without having to haul it up by the line, and it is gentler on the fish.
Things an angler uses.Fishing line: DuPont's nylon monofilament arrived in the late 1930s and replaced braided silk lines.
Things an angler uses.Fly: In fly fishing, this is a tiny lure of feathers, fur and thread that imitates an insect.
Things an angler uses.Waders: These waterproof overalls let an angler stand in a river, up to the chest.
Things an angler uses.Swivel: It prevents line twist, a small part that stops lines from tangling.
Things an angler uses.Saddle: Riders sit on it on horses, not on fishing trips.
Things an angler uses.Stirrups: Stirrups are for horse riders, not for anglers.
Things an angler uses.Shuttlecock: Used in badminton, the shuttlecock is not fishing gear.
Things an angler uses.Chalk bag: Climbers dust their hands with chalk bags, and it has no fishing role.
Things an angler uses.Carabiner: Carabiners are for climbers, not fishermen, though anglers may clip a net to a vest.
Things an angler uses.Belay device: A belay device is climbers' rope gear, which is not used when fishing.
Things an angler uses.Crampon: Crampons are spikes for icy mountains, not used in fishing.
Things an angler uses.Easel: Artists place canvases on easels, not anglers.
Things an angler uses.Kiln: Potters fire clay in a kiln, nothing to do with fishing.
Things an angler uses.Spindle: Used for spinning wool, the spindle has nothing to do with fishing, even if spinning reels share the word.
Things an angler uses.Trowel: The trowel is a builder's or gardener's tool, so a trap here, as only gardeners dig with it.

Surfing slang.Hang ten: Putting all ten toes over the nose of the board is a longboard stunt, and it only works when the board is trimmed just right in the wave.
Surfing slang.Barrel: Surfers chase the barrel because the wave curls over into a hollow tunnel, and riding inside it is called getting tubed.
Surfing slang.Wipeout: The word gave The Surfaris their 1963 instrumental hit, which opens with a manic laugh and a shouted title and a drum solo.
Surfing slang.Gnarly: Surfers of the 1960s borrowed it from gnarled, twisted things to mean dangerous waves, and it later grew into general slang.
Surfing slang.Tubular: Californian surfers used it for waves with a perfect barrel, and Valley Girl talk in the 1980s spread it as a word for great.
Surfing slang.Kook: This is a beginner who gets in the way, often by ignoring right-of-way rules in the lineup, and it's about the worst thing to be called.
Surfing slang.Swell: A swell is a train of waves made by distant storms, and ones that surfers ride may have crossed thousands of kilometers of open ocean.
Surfing slang.Duck dive: Paddling out, a surfer pushes the board nose under an oncoming wave and passes below it. Longboards are too buoyant to do it easily.
Surfing slang.Cutback: After racing ahead on a wave's face, a surfer turns sharply back toward the breaking part to regain power. It's one of surfing's basic maneuvers.
Surfing slang.Goofy foot: Riding with the right foot forward is called this. Roughly a quarter of surfers do it, and no one is sure how the name began.
Surfing slang.Shaka: The hang-loose sign, thumb and pinky out, comes from Hawaii, and a story credits a local sugar mill worker who lost three fingers.
Surfing slang.Point break: Waves that peel along a headland make long, regular rides, as at Jeffreys Bay in South Africa. A 1991 film borrowed the name.
Surfing slang.Moguls: These are the bumps on a ski slope, and freestyle skiers have competed over them at the Olympics since 1992. They aren't surfing.
Surfing slang.Slalom: The word comes from Norwegian for a sloping track. It's skiing, but surfers have no gates to weave between.
Surfing slang.Piste: Skiers use this French word for a marked, groomed trail. It originally meant a beaten track, and it's a snow term, not surf.
Surfing slang.Chairlift: The first ones were adapted from banana-loading equipment, and Sun Valley, Idaho installed the first ski chairlifts in 1936.
Surfing slang.Schuss: Skiers use this German word for straight downhill with no turning. It literally means shot, and has no place in the surf.
Surfing slang.Fairway: The mown strip between tee and green is golf turf, and the term came from the navigable channel of a waterway.
Surfing slang.Bunker: A sand trap in golf takes its name from the Scots word, once used for a coal chest, and it has no connection to waves.
Surfing slang.Wicket: Cricket's three stumps with two bails on top are called a wicket, and the same word also means a batter's turn at the crease.
Surfing slang.Dugout: The sunken shelter beside a baseball diamond was originally dug into the ground, hence the name, and it's not surf slang.
Surfing slang.Touchdown: American football's six-pointer originally needed the ball to be touched down on the ground. A scrum in rugby still works that way.
Surfing slang.Slap shot: This is a hockey shot with a big wind-up. Some players have launched them over 160 km/h, but it's not a surf move.
Surfing slang.Checkmate: The chess ending comes from Persian shah mat, often rendered as the king is helpless, and nothing to do with waves.

Associated with ancient Egypt.Pyramid: The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest human-made structure for around 3,800 years, until Lincoln Cathedral surpassed it.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Pharaoh: The title originally meant "great house" and referred to the palace. Only later did it name the king himself.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Mummy: Egyptians removed the brain through the nose, but left the heart in place since they thought it held thought and judgment.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Sphinx: The Great Sphinx at Giza has a lion's body and a human head, and was carved from a single ridge of limestone bedrock.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Papyrus: A reed from the Nile marshes pressed into sheets. The word "paper" comes from it, though papyrus is not true paper.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Hieroglyphics: Egyptian writing was undecipherable for centuries until the Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, let Champollion crack it in the 1820s.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Scarab: Dung beetles rolling balls of dung inspired this symbol of rebirth, as Egyptians pictured the sun being rolled across the sky.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Sarcophagus: The word comes from Greek for "flesh-eating," after a limestone believed to rot corpses quickly. It's the stone coffin.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Nile: The world's longest river, about 6,650 km, whose yearly floods fertilized the land and made Egyptian farming possible.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Ankh: This cross with a loop is the Egyptian symbol of life. Gods are often shown holding it to the noses of pharaohs.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Obelisk: A tall tapered stone pillar. More obelisks now stand in Rome than in Egypt, taken by emperors as trophies.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Canopic jar: Used to store the organs removed in mummification. Four jars, each with its own protective god, held liver, lungs, stomach and intestines.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Ziggurat: A stepped temple tower of Mesopotamia, such as Ur's. It's Sumerian and Babylonian, not Egyptian, though it resembles a pyramid.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Colosseum: Rome's great amphitheater, which could hold roughly 50,000 spectators. It is Roman and far later than the pyramids.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Parthenon: The temple of Athena on the Athenian Acropolis, finished in 432 BC. Greek, not Egyptian.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Toga: A draped wool garment of Roman citizens. Egyptians wore linen kilts and sheath dresses instead.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Samurai: Japan's warrior class, which lasted from about the 12th century until 1868. It has no link to ancient Egypt.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Runes: The angular alphabet of Germanic and Norse peoples, carved in stone and wood. Not an Egyptian script.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Totem pole: Carved cedar poles of Pacific Northwest Indigenous peoples that record family stories. They have no Egyptian connection.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Pagoda: A tiered tower common in East Asian temples, with roots in Indian stupas. Not Egyptian.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Longship: The sleek, shallow-drafted vessel of the Vikings, which could sail up rivers and land on beaches. Scandinavian.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Cuneiform: A trap: it's among the world's oldest writing systems, but it is Mesopotamian, pressed into clay with a reed, not Egyptian.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Terracotta Army: Thousands of life-size clay soldiers buried near China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang. Chinese, not Egyptian.
Associated with ancient Egypt.Stonehenge: The stone ring in England was begun around 3000 BC, with its huge stones raised later. It's older than some pyramids but unrelated.

Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Jason: Captain of the Argo, sent by his uncle Pelias to fetch the Golden Fleece from Colchis.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Heracles: The strongest hero joined the crew, but was left behind in Mysia when his companion Hylas was taken by nymphs.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Orpheus: The legendary musician played his lyre so beautifully on the voyage that it drowned out the Sirens' song and saved the crew.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Castor: A horse-taming twin, he joined with his brother Pollux, later the Gemini constellation.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Pollux: A boxer and twin of Castor, he beat King Amycus in a boxing match on the voyage.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Peleus: Father of Achilles, he married the sea nymph Thetis, whose wedding party led to the Trojan War.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Zetes: A son of the North Wind who, with his brother Calais, had wings and chased away the harpies tormenting King Phineus.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Calais: Winged son of Boreas, who helped drive off the Harpies, together with his brother Zetes.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Meleager: Hero of the Calydonian boar hunt, who joined the Argo and later died when a burning log tied to his life was cast in the fire.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Lynceus: His name means 'lynx-eyed', since he supposedly could see through the earth and spot far-off things.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Telamon: Father of Great Ajax, and a companion of Heracles, he joined the Argonauts.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Achilles: A trap: he was a baby, or not yet born, when the Argo sailed; his father Peleus was aboard.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Odysseus: A trap: the Ithacan hero was a child or unborn at the time of the Argo's voyage, and his own journey came after Troy.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Perseus: A trap: Perseus came a generation before Jason, and he killed Medusa without any ship or crew.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Hector: A trap: Troy's champion belongs to the Trojan War, which came a generation after the Argo's voyage.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Paris: A trap: the prince of Troy who took Helen lived in the generation after the Argonauts.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Agamemnon: A trap: the Greek commander at Troy belongs to a later generation, after the Argonauts sailed.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Ajax: A trap: Ajax was a hero at Troy, not on the Argo, though his father Telamon was an Argonaut.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Medea: The sorceress who helped Jason; she sailed with him afterward but wasn't a crew member.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Aeneas: A trap: the Trojan survivor who founded Rome in Virgil's tale belongs to the Trojan War era.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Bellerophon: A trap: the rider of Pegasus, who slew the Chimera, had his own adventures separate from the Argo.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Oedipus: A trap: the king of Thebes belongs to a separate tragic cycle, not the quest for the Golden Fleece.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Icarus: A trap: he flew on wax wings from Crete, a different story; the Argo's voyage is separate.
Argonauts (crew of the Argo).Minos: A trap: the Cretan king and his Labyrinth belong to the era of Theseus, not the Argo's crew.

Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Ziggurat: A stepped temple tower of mud brick, built to link earth with heaven. The Tower of Babel story may echo Babylon's great ziggurat.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Cuneiform: One of the first writing systems, made by pressing a reed stylus into wet clay. The name means "wedge-shaped" in Latin.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Hammurabi: A king of Babylon around 1750 BC whose law code, carved on a stone pillar, set penalties such as "an eye for an eye".
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Gilgamesh: The hero of the world's oldest known epic, a king of Uruk who seeks immortality after his friend Enkidu dies. It was written on clay tablets.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Babylon: The city whose Ishtar Gate was blue and covered in glazed brick. The Hanging Gardens attributed to it may never have existed there.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Ur: A Sumerian city in southern Iraq, birthplace of Abraham according to the Bible. Royal tombs there held gold treasures and sacrificed attendants.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Sumer: Early southern Mesopotamia, where writing, the wheel, and the first cities may have arisen. Its name means "land of the civilised kings".
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Nineveh: The capital of Assyria and site of Ashurbanipal's great library. It is also the city where the Bible's Jonah was sent to preach.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Tigris: One of the two rivers framing Mesopotamia. Its name came into Greek from an old Persian word meaning "arrow", for its fast flow.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Euphrates: Western Asia's longest river, about 2,800 km, it also bounded Mesopotamia, whose name means "between rivers".
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Assyria: A fierce empire that, at its height in the 7th century BC, ruled from Egypt to Iran. Its kings kept lion-hunt reliefs in their palaces.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Akkad: Home of Sargon, who around 2300 BC created what is often called the first empire. Akkadian became a major language of the region.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Uruk: Perhaps the world's first true city, with maybe 40,000 people around 3000 BC. It gave Iraq its modern name, some believe.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Pyramids of Giza: Egyptian, not Mesopotamian. The Great Pyramid, built for Khufu around 2560 BC, was the tallest human-made structure for nearly 4,000 years.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Sphinx: A limestone guardian in Egypt, carved with a pharaoh's face, probably Khafre's. Mesopotamia had winged guardians too, but this one is Egyptian.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Hieroglyphs: Egypt's picture-writing system, deciphered in the 1820s by Champollion with the Rosetta Stone. Mesopotamia used cuneiform instead.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Nile: The Egyptian river, flowing north some 6,650 km. Mesopotamia belonged to the Tigris and Euphrates, a neighbouring region.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Acropolis: Athens's famous hill of Greek temples. It belongs to classical Greece, more than 2,000 years after Sumer's first cities.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Colosseum: A Roman amphitheatre completed in AD 80, a world apart in time and place from Mesopotamia.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Machu Picchu: An Inca citadel high in Peru, built in the 1400s. It is in the Americas, with no contact with Mesopotamia.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Great Wall: A Chinese defensive wall system, built over many centuries. It is East Asian and unrelated to Mesopotamia.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Stonehenge: A British stone circle, started around 3000 BC, so it is about as old as the first cities in Sumer, though thousands of miles from it.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Petra: The Nabataean rock city in Jordan, carved around the 1st century BC. It is later than Mesopotamia's glory days by thousands of years.
Associated with ancient Mesopotamia.Angkor Wat: A 12th-century Cambodian temple. The Khmer built it thousands of years after Mesopotamia's great age.

Things that are usually round.Plate: Round plates let a diner rotate food easily and are the easiest shape to stack, and some ancient plates were made from bread.
Things that are usually round.Coin: Most coins are round so they roll through machines and wear evenly, though a few countries have made square or wavy ones.
Things that are usually round.Pizza: Pizza is round because dough tossed in the air spins into a disc, and the Neapolitan version dates to 18th-century Naples.
Things that are usually round.Wheel: The oldest known wheels were used by potters in Mesopotamia around 3500 BCE, before anyone put them on carts.
Things that are usually round.Button: Buttons were first used for decoration, and the buttonhole came centuries later, in 13th-century Germany.
Things that are usually round.Doughnut: The hole is there so the middle cooks as fast as the outside, which a solid fried ball of dough does not do.
Things that are usually round.CD: A CD is read by a laser from the underside, and the audio is stored as a spiral track of microscopic pits.
Things that are usually round.Frisbee: The Frisbee began as a pie tin from the Frisbie Baking Company that college students tossed around, and the toy was later renamed.
Things that are usually round.Wedding ring: The ring's unbroken circle is a symbol of endless love, and exchanging rings goes back to ancient Egypt.
Things that are usually round.Jar lid: Round lids work because a circle can screw on in any orientation, and a square one never could.
Things that are usually round.Dartboard: The standard dartboard numbers are arranged so that big numbers sit beside small ones, punishing a wild throw.
Things that are usually round.Hula hoop: Hula hoops took off in 1958 when Wham-O sold tens of millions in a few months, and hoops themselves date back to ancient times.
Things that are usually round.Bagel: Bagels are boiled briefly before baking, and this is what gives the shiny crust and chewy texture.
Things that are usually round.Book: Books are rectangular, so they stack neatly on a shelf, and a round book would be impractical to store.
Things that are usually round.Door: Doors are usually rectangles, which fit people and furniture, though round doors do exist, like the one in a hobbit hole.
Things that are usually round.Envelope: Envelopes are normally rectangles folded from a diamond-shaped sheet, the origin of the pointed flap.
Things that are usually round.Ruler: A ruler is a long, flat strip, and its shape is made to measure straight lines.
Things that are usually round.Brick: Bricks are rectangles because they stack with interlocking joints, and a standard one is made to be gripped in one hand.
Things that are usually round.Smartphone: Smartphones are rectangles with rounded corners, a shape that fits a hand and a pocket and a rectangular screen.
Things that are usually round.Laptop: A laptop is a flat rectangle when closed, and its shape is chosen to match the screen and keyboard.
Things that are usually round.Credit card: Credit cards are rectangles of a standardized size, and the same size is used all over the world for payment and ID.
Things that are usually round.Postage stamp: Stamps are usually small rectangles with perforated edges, and the first one, the Penny Black, appeared in 1840.
Things that are usually round.Chessboard: A chessboard is square, with 64 alternating squares, and the checkered pattern helps a player track diagonals.
Things that are usually round.Sticky note: Sticky notes are mostly squares, and the first widely sold pad was a pale yellow because of scrap paper at 3M.

Things that have a lens.Camera: The word camera comes from camera obscura, Latin for 'dark room', and the lens is the heart of any camera.
Things that have a lens.Eyeglasses: Eyeglasses were invented in northern Italy in the late 1200s, and for centuries each lens was made by hand.
Things that have a lens.Telescope: Hans Lippershey applied for a patent on a telescope in 1608, and Galileo built his own version within a year.
Things that have a lens.Microscope: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek used tiny single lenses to spot bacteria in the 1670s, calling them 'animalcules'.
Things that have a lens.Magnifying glass: A magnifying glass is a single convex lens, and it can also focus sunlight to start a fire.
Things that have a lens.Binoculars: Binoculars pair two telescopes with prisms, which flip the image upright and fold the long light path into a short tube.
Things that have a lens.Projector: A projector uses lenses to throw a tiny bright image onto a large screen.
Things that have a lens.Webcam: The first webcam, at Cambridge University in 1991, watched a coffee pot so researchers would know if it had coffee.
Things that have a lens.Door peephole: A peephole uses a wide-angle lens to give a view of about 180 degrees from just a tiny hole.
Things that have a lens.Human eye: The eye's lens is transparent protein that stiffens with age, which is why most people need reading glasses in middle age.
Things that have a lens.Lighthouse: Augustin Fresnel's 1820s lens, made of ringed glass prisms, let lighthouse beams reach dozens of miles to sea.
Things that have a lens.Smartphone: Many phones carry three or four tiny lenses, each doing a different job such as zoom, wide shots or depth.
Things that have a lens.Mirror: A mirror reflects light but does not bend it to focus, which is the difference between mirror and lens.
Things that have a lens.Window: A window is flat glass that lets light through without focusing it, so it is not a lens.
Things that have a lens.Prism: A prism splits white light into a rainbow, but it does not focus it into an image.
Things that have a lens.Light bulb: A bulb's glass is just a cover, and it is shaped to contain the filament, not to focus light.
Things that have a lens.Hourglass: An hourglass is shaped glass that holds sand, and it does not focus or magnify.
Things that have a lens.Wine glass: A wine glass's curve can distort what you see through it, though it does not form a lens in practice.
Things that have a lens.Snow globe: The water in a snow globe actually works as a lens, magnifying the figure, but the globe is not a lens by design.
Things that have a lens.Picture frame: A frame's glass is flat, so it protects without magnifying or focusing the picture.
Things that have a lens.Wall clock: The flat glass cover on a wall clock lets you see the hands without bending the light.
Things that have a lens.Compass: Some baseplate compasses include a small magnifier, but the compass itself is a magnetic needle.
Things that have a lens.Calculator: A calculator uses chips and a screen, no lens needed, though a solar strip does catch light.
Things that have a lens.Radio: A radio picks up waves with an antenna and a tuner, none of which involve a lens.

Settings on a washing machine.Spin: Fast drum spin presses water out with centrifugal force, and top-end machines spin at 1,400 revolutions per minute or more.
Settings on a washing machine.Rinse: A rinse cycle flushes out detergent, and leftover soap is a common reason clothes feel stiff or irritate skin.
Settings on a washing machine.Delicates: The gentle cycle uses slow tumbling and cool water, and a mesh bag protects lace and bras from snagging.
Settings on a washing machine.Cotton: Cotton can handle hot water and long cycles, but a hot wash is what shrinks it, so many people choose 40 degrees.
Settings on a washing machine.Quick wash: A 15-minute cycle works for lightly worn clothes, and it saves energy but not for heavily soiled items.
Settings on a washing machine.Wool: Wool shrinks and felts with heat and agitation, so the wool cycle is slow and cool, and it is how a favorite sweater is spared.
Settings on a washing machine.Synthetics: Synthetic fabrics shed microplastic fibers in the wash, and a filter bag can catch some of them.
Settings on a washing machine.Eco: Eco cycles run longer at lower temperatures, since heating the water takes most of the energy a wash uses.
Settings on a washing machine.Hand wash: The hand wash setting mimics a gentle by-hand scrub, with minimal drum movement for items with that label.
Settings on a washing machine.Heavy duty: Heavy duty cycles use more agitation and hot water for towels, work clothes and muddy sports kit.
Settings on a washing machine.Bedding: Duvets and comforters need a big drum and extra rinse, since they trap soap and water.
Settings on a washing machine.Prewash: A prewash adds a short first wash before the main one, useful for muddy or stained loads.
Settings on a washing machine.Defrost: This is a microwave setting, where it thaws frozen food by pulsing power so it doesn't cook the edges.
Settings on a washing machine.Bake: Oven setting, and the bottom heating element does the work, so a washing machine has no use for it.
Settings on a washing machine.Grill: The oven's top element radiates direct heat to brown food, nothing a washing machine does.
Settings on a washing machine.Popcorn: Microwaves have a popcorn button, though experts recommend stopping when pops slow to two seconds apart.
Settings on a washing machine.Reheat: This is a microwave key, and the washer never has a reason to heat leftovers.
Settings on a washing machine.Toast: A toaster has a toast dial, and the setting controls how long the element glows.
Settings on a washing machine.Broil: American for grill, and it exists on ovens, not on laundry machines.
Settings on a washing machine.Pulse: A blender's pulse button chops in short bursts, which is how you keep salsa chunky rather than pureed.
Settings on a washing machine.Blend: A blender setting, and the speed controls how fast the blade turns.
Settings on a washing machine.Crush ice: Some blenders have a special setting that alternates blade speeds to break up ice cubes.
Settings on a washing machine.Brew: A coffee maker's brew button heats water and pumps it through the grounds, not through your laundry.
Settings on a washing machine.Espresso: Espresso machines force near-boiling water through fine grounds at about nine bars of pressure, much more than washers ever see.

Types of bacteria.E. coli: Most E. coli strains live harmlessly in your gut; only a few, like O157:H7, cause serious illness.
Types of bacteria.Salmonella: Named after the American veterinarian Daniel Salmon, whose research team isolated it in the 1880s.
Types of bacteria.Listeria: Listeria can multiply at refrigerator temperatures, which is why pregnant people are warned off deli meats and soft cheeses.
Types of bacteria.Staphylococcus: The name means 'grape cluster', after how its round cells clump, and many people carry it harmlessly on their skin.
Types of bacteria.Streptococcus: Its cells line up in chains, hence a name from Greek for 'twisted chain', and one species causes strep throat.
Types of bacteria.Lactobacillus: These bacteria ferment sugars into lactic acid, which gives yogurt and sauerkraut their tang.
Types of bacteria.Clostridium: Clostridium botulinum makes botulinum toxin, among the most potent poisons known, and Botox is a purified form of it.
Types of bacteria.Bifidobacterium: Bifidobacteria are among the first gut settlers in breastfed babies, feeding on sugars in human milk.
Types of bacteria.Vibrio cholerae: This comma-shaped bacterium causes cholera, and John Snow traced an 1854 London outbreak to one water pump.
Types of bacteria.Influenza: Influenza is a virus, so antibiotics do nothing against it, though they treat bacterial complications.
Types of bacteria.Rhinovirus: Rhinovirus is a virus and the leading cause of the common cold, with over 100 types.
Types of bacteria.Norovirus: The 'cruise ship stomach bug' is a virus, and a tiny number of particles can make someone ill.
Types of bacteria.HIV: HIV is a virus that attacks immune cells, which is why antibiotics cannot treat it.
Types of bacteria.Ebola: Ebola is a virus named after a river in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Types of bacteria.Rabies: Rabies is a virus that travels along nerves to the brain, and is almost always fatal once symptoms begin.
Types of bacteria.Measles: Measles is a virus so contagious that one case can infect most unvaccinated people nearby.
Types of bacteria.Coronavirus: Coronaviruses are viruses named for crown-like spikes, 'corona' meaning crown in Latin.
Types of bacteria.Herpes: Herpes viruses are lifelong guests, hiding in nerve cells after the first infection.
Types of bacteria.Zika: Zika is a virus named for a forest in Uganda where it was first identified in 1947.
Types of bacteria.Yeast: Yeast is a single-celled fungus, a cousin of mushrooms, not a bacterium.
Types of bacteria.Mold: Mold is a fungus rather than bacteria, spreading by spores that drift through the air.
Types of bacteria.Penicillium: It is a mold, not bacteria, and from it Alexander Fleming's 1928 discovery gave us penicillin.
Types of bacteria.Candida: Candida is a yeast, a fungus, that lives harmlessly in many people but can cause thrush.
Types of bacteria.Amoeba: An amoeba is a single-celled organism with a nucleus, which bacteria lack.

Body parts that grow back.Hair: Scalp hair grows about a centimeter a month, in growth cycles that last for years before each hair sheds.
Body parts that grow back.Fingernails: Fingernails regrow completely in about half a year, which is noticeably faster than toenails do.
Body parts that grow back.Toenails: Toenails take a year or more to regrow, much slower than fingernails, so a lost one is a long wait.
Body parts that grow back.Skin: Your outer skin renews itself roughly every month, so the surface you see is constantly being replaced.
Body parts that grow back.Eyelashes: Eyelashes are replaced every couple of months, and the upper lid carries around a hundred of them.
Body parts that grow back.Eyebrows: Eyebrow hairs are replaced every few months, though overplucked brows sometimes never fully return.
Body parts that grow back.Liver: A beard grows about half an inch a month, driven by hormones, and shaving does not make it grow thicker.
Body parts that grow back.Stomach lining: The liver can regenerate from as little as a quarter of its tissue, which makes living-donor transplants possible.
Body parts that grow back.Beard: The stomach lining renews itself every few days, which lets it survive in a bath of strong acid.
Body parts that grow back.Adult teeth: Adult teeth do not regrow once lost, unlike sharks, which replace their teeth continually through life.
Body parts that grow back.Fingers: A child's fingertip can regrow if the nail base remains, but whole fingers and adult tips cannot.
Body parts that grow back.Arm: Starfish and salamanders regrow limbs, but a human arm lost to injury cannot grow back on its own.
Body parts that grow back.Kidney: Kidneys cannot regrow, which is why donating one leaves a single kidney that works harder.
Body parts that grow back.Eyeball: Some salamanders can regrow the lens of the eye, but a human eyeball never regenerates.
Body parts that grow back.Appendix: Once surgically removed, the appendix does not return, and people live healthy lives without it.
Body parts that grow back.Ear: Ear cartilage cannot regrow, so a lost ear requires surgical reconstruction using cartilage from elsewhere.
Body parts that grow back.Nose: Nose tissue does not regrow, so a lost nose needs reconstruction, often using skin and cartilage from the body.
Body parts that grow back.Toe: Toes do not regrow, though toenails do, and the lost digit can only be replaced by a prosthetic.
Body parts that grow back.Tongue: Taste buds replace themselves every week or two, but a lost piece of tongue stays lost, though it heals fast.
Body parts that grow back.Leg: Legs do not regrow; lizards can regrow lost tails, but humans have no such ability.
Body parts that grow back.Earlobe: Torn earlobes do not regrow on their own, though surgeons can repair them neatly.
Body parts that grow back.Heart: Heart muscle cells barely renew, so heart attack scars are permanent, whereas zebrafish can regrow heart tissue.
Body parts that grow back.Thumb: A thumb does not regrow, though microsurgery can sometimes reattach one if it is preserved properly.
Body parts that grow back.Lung: Lungs cannot regrow, though the remaining tissue can adapt a little after surgery.

Things you'd find in a barn.Hay bale: A tightly packed block of dried grass for winter feed. Hay stacked wet can heat up and even spontaneously catch fire.
Things you'd find in a barn.Pitchfork: Used for lifting hay and straw. Its long tines make it fit for forking loose bundles, and gave the cartoon devil his prop.
Things you'd find in a barn.Saddle: Stored in barns on racks. Western saddles can weigh 30 pounds or more, much heavier than lightweight English saddles.
Things you'd find in a barn.Horse stall: A compartment where a horse rests. Horses can doze standing up thanks to a locking mechanism in their legs.
Things you'd find in a barn.Feed trough: A container for livestock food or water. The word 'trough' also names the lowest point of a wave or a cycle.
Things you'd find in a barn.Hayloft: The upper storage floor of a barn. Hay was dropped down through a hatch to animals below.
Things you'd find in a barn.Bridle: Part of a horse's headgear, and it holds the bit. Reins attach to the bridle, which is how riders steer.
Things you'd find in a barn.Milking stool: A low three-legged stool lets a farmer sit beside a cow. Three legs stay steady on uneven barn floors.
Things you'd find in a barn.Harness: Gear that lets draft horses pull wagons or ploughs. A well-fitted collar is key to preventing choking.
Things you'd find in a barn.Horseshoe: Nailed to hooves, shoes protect them on hard ground. Hanging one over a door is a lucky tradition.
Things you'd find in a barn.Stethoscope: A doctor's tool, found in clinics. The first one, built by René Laennec in 1816, was a simple wooden tube.
Things you'd find in a barn.Chandelier: A hanging light for grand rooms. The word comes from French for candle holder.
Things you'd find in a barn.Jacuzzi: A hot tub brand named after a family of Italian-American inventors, and a home luxury rather than a barn feature.
Things you'd find in a barn.Grand piano: A concert-hall instrument weighing hundreds of pounds. An out-of-place sight in a barn, except in stunts.
Things you'd find in a barn.Escalator: A moving staircase for malls and stations. 'Escalator' began as a trademark, and was later made generic by a court.
Things you'd find in a barn.Vending machine: Self-service sales machines date back to ancient Egypt, where one reportedly dispensed holy water for coins.
Things you'd find in a barn.Treadmill: Originally punishment machines in Victorian prisons, they now belong in gyms. A barn would be an odd site.
Things you'd find in a barn.Pool table: Table games are for pubs and halls. Pool tables are traditionally covered in felt, not leather.
Things you'd find in a barn.Cash register: Invented in 1879 by a saloon owner who wanted to stop employee theft. A shop item, not a barn one.
Things you'd find in a barn.Photocopier: Chester Carlson's xerography process dates to 1938. Offices use copiers, not farms.
Things you'd find in a barn.Hospital bed: Medical beds with adjustable frames fit hospitals. A barn bed would more likely be a bed of straw.
Things you'd find in a barn.Bunsen burner: A lab gas burner, named after chemist Robert Bunsen. It's for classrooms and laboratories.
Things you'd find in a barn.Ballot box: Polling places use these to collect votes. The word 'ballot' comes from the Italian for little ball, as voting once used balls.
Things you'd find in a barn.Espresso machine: Italy's invention for fast coffee, found in cafes. Angelo Moriondo patented an early version in 1884.

Things a photographer uses.Camera: The word camera comes from camera obscura, Latin for "dark room," the pinhole device that predates film.
Things a photographer uses.Tripod: A tripod keeps the camera still in long exposures, and photographers use it to capture silky waterfalls or starry skies.
Things a photographer uses.Lens: A lens bends light onto the sensor, and a wide aperture lets in more light to blur the background.
Things a photographer uses.Flash: A flash can freeze fast motion, and the first ones used burning magnesium powder, which was quite dangerous.
Things a photographer uses.Light meter: A light meter measures the brightness so the photographer can choose settings, and it was key before cameras had one built in.
Things a photographer uses.Memory card: A single modern card can hold thousands of high-resolution photos, far more than rolls of film ever did.
Things a photographer uses.Softbox: A softbox diffuses the light and makes shadows gentler, giving portraits a flattering look.
Things a photographer uses.Reflector: A reflector bounces light to fill in shadows, and it can be as simple as a piece of white card.
Things a photographer uses.Lens cap: A lens cap keeps dust and scratches off the glass, and it is famously the first thing photographers lose.
Things a photographer uses.Shutter release: A remote or cable release lets you take a photo without touching the camera, avoiding blur from shake.
Things a photographer uses.Camera bag: Many photographers say the best camera bag looks unlike one, so thieves aren't tempted.
Things a photographer uses.Easel: An easel holds a painter's canvas, while photographers capture images with a lens.
Things a photographer uses.Palette: A palette is for mixing paints, and though a photo editor has a color palette too, it is not physical.
Things a photographer uses.Stethoscope: A stethoscope is for hearing the heart and lungs, so it's a doctor's tool.
Things a photographer uses.Kiln: A kiln fires clay and pottery, and a photographer's darkroom is the opposite of such heat.
Things a photographer uses.Loom: A loom weaves fabric, and is a weaver's tool.
Things a photographer uses.Anvil: An anvil is for forging metal, and a blacksmith's tool rather than a photographer's.
Things a photographer uses.Chisel: A chisel carves wood or stone, and is a sculptor's or carpenter's tool.
Things a photographer uses.Potter's wheel: A potter's wheel spins clay into pots, a craft far from photography.
Things a photographer uses.Spinning wheel: A spinning wheel makes thread from fiber, so it's a textile tool.
Things a photographer uses.Gavel: A gavel is for a judge or auctioneer, not for taking pictures.
Things a photographer uses.Trowel: A trowel is for gardening or masonry, though a photographer may kneel in dirt for a shot.
Things a photographer uses.Whisk: A whisk beats eggs and cream in a kitchen, though food photographers do capture it.
Things a photographer uses.Plunger: A plunger unclogs drains, which is a very different kind of job.

Words for a beginner at work.Trainee: A trainee is learning the job while working, a common way to enter careers from banking to plumbing in many countries.
Words for a beginner at work.Intern: The word comes from internes, junior doctors who lived inside the hospital. Today's internships are mostly offices, and often unpaid.
Words for a beginner at work.Novice: Novice comes from Latin novus, new, and it's also the term for someone preparing to take religious vows.
Words for a beginner at work.Rookie: Rookie may come from a corruption of recruit, and it was used in the British army by the 1800s before baseball adopted it.
Words for a beginner at work.Apprentice: Medieval apprenticeships lasted about seven years, and a guild required the apprentice to produce a masterpiece before becoming a master.
Words for a beginner at work.Newbie: Newbie is slang that started in the 1900s in British and American military use, and spread online as a jokey label.
Words for a beginner at work.Greenhorn: A greenhorn was originally a young ox with soft new horns, and the word became slang for an inexperienced person, especially on the American frontier.
Words for a beginner at work.Beginner: The word beginner is plain English, though in Zen Buddhism the beginner's mind is considered an advantage: open to everything.
Words for a beginner at work.Recruit: Recruit comes from French recrue, new growth, as in a plant sprouting again, and began as a word for fresh soldiers.
Words for a beginner at work.Cadet: Cadet comes from French for a younger son, because noble younger sons often entered the army, rather than inheriting the family estate.
Words for a beginner at work.Tenderfoot: Tenderfoot was frontier slang for newcomers whose feet weren't toughened to rough terrain, and later became Boy Scouts' beginner rank.
Words for a beginner at work.Veteran: A veteran comes from Latin vetus, old: it's the opposite of a beginner, which makes it the trap in this list.
Words for a beginner at work.Expert: An expert is the opposite of a beginner. Studies suggest it takes around 10,000 hours of practice, though the exact number is debated.
Words for a beginner at work.Master: A master was once the top of the guild ladder, above the journeyman who had moved up from apprentice.
Words for a beginner at work.Guru: Guru is Sanskrit for teacher, and literally means heavy, someone weighty with knowledge, so it describes an expert, not a newcomer.
Words for a beginner at work.Old hand: An old hand is a long-experienced worker, a naval phrase for sailors who knew the ship, and the opposite of a greenhorn.
Words for a beginner at work.Boss: Boss comes from Dutch baas, meaning master, and came into American English in the 1600s when its use was to avoid saying master.
Words for a beginner at work.Maestro: Maestro is Italian for master, and orchestras use it for conductors, even though it can mean a highly skilled person in any field.
Words for a beginner at work.Virtuoso: A virtuoso is a person of exceptional skill, from Italian for skilled or virtuous, once used for scholars and artists.
Words for a beginner at work.Elder: Elder is the opposite of the novice: a person with seniority and wisdom, as in tribal elders or church elders.
Words for a beginner at work.Senior partner: A senior partner is at the top of a law or accounting firm, and the very opposite of a trainee.
Words for a beginner at work.Chief: Chief comes from Latin caput, head, which is also the origin of the word capital and the word cattle.
Words for a beginner at work.Old-timer: An old-timer is a person who's been around for ages, so the opposite of a rookie, and often a source of workplace stories.
Words for a beginner at work.Mentor: Mentor was a character in Homer's Odyssey, a friend of Odysseus who advised his son Telemachus, so the word means an experienced guide.

Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows 95: Windows 95 introduced the Start button and taskbar in 1995. Microsoft's launch used the Rolling Stones' Start Me Up and had people queuing at midnight.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows 98: Windows 98 added USB support and was released in 1998. Its demo famously crashed with a blue screen when Bill Gates showed it live.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows XP: Windows XP (2001) lasted so long that millions kept using it past 2014, when official support ended. The XP stands for experience.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows Vista: Vista (2007) was criticized for slow performance and constant security prompts. It's remembered as one of Microsoft's most unpopular releases.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows 7: Windows 7 (2009) won back fans after Vista and stayed popular for years. Official support ended in January 2020.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows 8: Windows 8 (2012) removed the classic Start button in favor of a tile-based screen. Users disliked it, and it was partly reversed with 8.1.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows 10: Windows 10 (2015) was billed as the "last version of Windows," with updates instead of new numbers. Microsoft then released Windows 11.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows 11: Windows 11 arrived in 2021 with a centered taskbar and stricter hardware requirements. It followed Windows 10 and ignored the number 9.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows ME: Windows Millennium Edition (2000) was so unstable that many called it one of the worst. It was the last of the DOS-based Windows line.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows 2000: Windows 2000 was built on the NT line and brought business-grade stability. It was aimed at offices, not home users, and led to Windows XP.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows 1.0: Windows 1.0 arrived in 1985 as a graphical shell for MS-DOS. Its windows were tiled, because overlapping windows came in version 2.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows 3.1: Windows 3.1 (1992) added TrueType fonts, so text looked the same on screen and in print. It sold tens of millions of copies and brought many people to PCs.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows 9: Microsoft skipped Windows 9 and went straight from 8 to 10. One theory is that old code checking for names starting with "Windows 9" would mistake it for 95 or 98.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows 99: Windows 99 never existed. Microsoft went from 98 to 2000 and ME.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows 96: Windows 96 isn't real. Windows 95 came out in 1995, and its name pattern shows the year, but there was never a 96.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows XL: Windows XL is made up. Microsoft's Excel is a spreadsheet program, not a Windows version.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows Pro Max: Windows Pro Max sounds like an Apple-style name and isn't a Windows edition. Real ones are called Home, Pro, Enterprise and so on.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows Galaxy: Windows Galaxy never existed. Galaxy is Samsung's phone brand, not a Microsoft release.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows Leopard: Leopard belongs to Apple's Mac OS X from 2007. Windows never had a version with that name, though Windows Vista was its rival at the time.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows Ice: Windows Ice isn't a real version. Microsoft's actual codenames included Longhorn, Whistler and Chicago.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows 97: Windows 97 never existed. The 95 version was followed by 98, skipping 97 entirely.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows Sierra: Sierra is a macOS name from 2016, not a Windows one. Mixed-up brands make a good trap.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows Turbo: Windows Turbo isn't a real release. Turbo is a name more common to Borland's programming tools of the same era.
Real versions of Microsoft Windows.Windows Max: Windows Max never existed. Real Windows names follow a number, a year or a short word, not a made-up suffix.

Plays written by Shakespeare.Hamlet: The ghost on the battlements, the prince's delay and the graveyard skull help make it one of the most famous plays ever.
Plays written by Shakespeare.Macbeth: The shortest of the tragedies, and the play actors superstitiously call 'the Scottish play'.
Plays written by Shakespeare.Othello: Its villain Iago is one of Shakespeare's most famous manipulators.
Plays written by Shakespeare.Cymbeline: A late romance set in ancient Britain with a wager, a disguise, and a lost heir.
