Plays written by Shakespeare.Pericles: Pericles is co-written, probably with George Wilkins, and tells an adventure at sea.
Plays written by Shakespeare.Coriolanus: A Roman tragedy of a proud general who cannot flatter the crowd.
Plays written by Shakespeare.The Tempest: His last solo-authored play, often read as a farewell to the stage.
Plays written by Shakespeare.Twelfth Night: A comedy of twins, shipwreck, and cross-dressing, its subtitle is 'What You Will'.
Plays written by Shakespeare.Henry V: A history play with the Saint Crispin's Day speech.
Plays written by Shakespeare.Richard III: The play opens with 'Now is the winter of our discontent', one of the most famous openings in English.
Plays written by Shakespeare.King John: A history play that few people see, though it is by Shakespeare.
Plays written by Shakespeare.As You Like It: A comedy featuring 'All the world's a stage', set in the forest of Arden.
Plays written by Shakespeare.Measure for Measure: A dark comedy sometimes called a problem play, by Shakespeare despite its grim tone.
Plays written by Shakespeare.Doctor Faustus: Christopher Marlowe's tragedy of a scholar who sells his soul to the devil, not Shakespeare's.
Plays written by Shakespeare.Volpone: Ben Jonson's satire of greed, in which three men flatter a rich man hoping to be his heir.
Plays written by Shakespeare.The Alchemist: Ben Jonson's The Alchemist is a comic swindle set in a plague-emptied London house, and not by Shakespeare.
Plays written by Shakespeare.Tartuffe: Molière's comedy about a con man pretending to be pious, in French and not Shakespeare's.
Plays written by Shakespeare.Hedda Gabler: Henrik Ibsen's 1890 play about a woman trapped in a stifling marriage, by a Norwegian.
Plays written by Shakespeare.A Doll's House: Ibsen's 1879 play ends with Nora walking out of her marriage, which shocked audiences.
Plays written by Shakespeare.Waiting for Godot: Samuel Beckett's play about two men waiting for someone who never arrives is not Shakespeare.
Plays written by Shakespeare.The Seagull: Chekhov's 1896 play, in which a young actress and a seagull share a symbolism, is not Shakespeare.
Plays written by Shakespeare.Pygmalion: George Bernard Shaw's play that inspired the musical My Fair Lady.
Plays written by Shakespeare.Medea: Euripides wrote this Greek tragedy of a vengeful sorceress, not Shakespeare.
Plays written by Shakespeare.Antigone: A Greek tragedy by Sophocles about a woman who defies a king to bury her brother, not Shakespeare.

Good conductors of electricity.Copper: Copper is the standard for household wiring, and only silver conducts electricity better.
Good conductors of electricity.Silver: Silver is the best electrical conductor of any metal, but it's too expensive for general wiring.
Good conductors of electricity.Gold: Gold doesn't corrode, so it coats electrical contacts in phones and computers.
Good conductors of electricity.Aluminum: Overhead power lines are mostly aluminum, which is lighter and cheaper than copper for the same current.
Good conductors of electricity.Iron: Iron conducts electricity, but roughly six times worse than copper, and it rusts.
Good conductors of electricity.Salt water: Pure water barely conducts, but dissolved salt ions carry the current, which is why salt water is a hazard in electrical accidents.
Good conductors of electricity.Graphite: Graphite is carbon, a nonmetal, yet it conducts thanks to free electrons between its layers, while diamond doesn't.
Good conductors of electricity.Steel: Steel conducts less well than copper, so high-voltage lines often have a steel core for strength wrapped in aluminum.
Good conductors of electricity.Mercury: Mercury is the only metal liquid at room temperature, and it conducts well, which is why it was used in old tilt switches.
Good conductors of electricity.Brass: Brass is copper and zinc, and it's used for plug pins because it's conductive and resists corrosion.
Good conductors of electricity.Platinum: Platinum resists corrosion, and its resistance changes predictably with temperature, so it's used in precision thermometers.
Good conductors of electricity.Rubber: Electricians' gloves are rubber for a reason, and they're tested at high voltages to be sure.
Good conductors of electricity.Glass: Glass insulates at room temperature, but heated until it glows it becomes a conductor.
Good conductors of electricity.Plastic: Plastics are classic insulators, but conducting polymers were discovered and won a Nobel Prize in 2000.
Good conductors of electricity.Dry wood: Dry wood insulates, but wet wood conducts enough to be dangerous, which is why ladders for electricians are fiberglass.
Good conductors of electricity.Cotton: Cotton insulates when dry, but a soaked cotton rag can conduct enough to cause a shock.
Good conductors of electricity.Porcelain: Porcelain insulators on power poles keep high-voltage wires from touching the structure.
Good conductors of electricity.Air: Air is an insulator until the voltage gets high enough, and lightning is air suddenly breaking down.
Good conductors of electricity.Paper: Paper soaked in oil was used to insulate power cables for decades.
Good conductors of electricity.Wool: Wool is an insulator, which is why rubbing it builds up static charge that can't drain away.
Good conductors of electricity.Diamond: Diamond is an electrical insulator but one of the best heat conductors known.
Good conductors of electricity.Styrofoam: Styrofoam insulates against both heat and electricity, and it's mostly trapped air.
Good conductors of electricity.Candle wax: Paraffin wax is a good electrical insulator, even though it's soft and melts easily.
Good conductors of electricity.Distilled water: Pure water is a poor conductor; the dissolved minerals and ions in ordinary water do the work.

Stretchy things.Rubber band: The rubber band was patented in England in 1845 by Stephen Perry.
Stretchy things.Leggings: The stretch in leggings comes from spandex woven in with cotton or nylon.
Stretchy things.Bungee cord: Bungee jumping drew inspiration from Vanuatu's land-diving ritual, where jumpers tie vines to their ankles.
Stretchy things.Balloon: A balloon is hardest to blow up at the start and gets easier once the rubber has stretched.
Stretchy things.Chewing gum: Gum base today is synthetic rubber, a long way from the tree resins chewed by ancient people.
Stretchy things.Hair tie: The scrunchie was invented in 1987 by Rommy Revson.
Stretchy things.Slinky: The Slinky was invented by accident in 1943 by naval engineer Richard James.
Stretchy things.Resistance band: Resistance bands began as physical therapy gear.
Stretchy things.Silly Putty: Silly Putty was invented by accident during World War II rubber research, and it can bounce, stretch and copy newsprint.
Stretchy things.Latex glove: Latex gloves came into surgery around 1890, reportedly after a nurse at Johns Hopkins asked for them.
Stretchy things.Swim cap: Swim caps made of latex or silicone stretch over the head and reduce drag.
Stretchy things.Elastic waistband: Elastic waistbands are woven with rubber or spandex threads that spring back after stretching.
Stretchy things.Chain: A chain is flexible but not stretchy, because its links hold strength rather than give.
Stretchy things.Pencil: Hexagonal pencils are common partly because they're easy to grip and don't roll off tables.
Stretchy things.Cardboard: Corrugated cardboard has fluting that adds stiffness and strength, not stretch.
Stretchy things.Brick: Bricks bear huge compression but crack when stretched.
Stretchy things.Wooden ruler: A wooden ruler can flex, but it won't stretch, and it snaps if bent too far.
Stretchy things.Paper: Paper tears rather than stretches, and it was invented in China around 105 CE.
Stretchy things.Cracker: Brittle foods fracture rather than stretch, which is where the crack in cracker comes from.
Stretchy things.Ceramic bowl: Fired clay is hard but brittle, and stretching it breaks it.
Stretchy things.Ice cube: Ice shatters rather than stretches, although glaciers do flow very slowly.
Stretchy things.Chalk: Natural chalk is soft limestone made of microscopic marine plankton shells, as in the cliffs of Dover.
Stretchy things.Popsicle stick: A popsicle stick bends but doesn't stretch, and snaps if you push it too far.
Stretchy things.Credit card: A credit card flexes and bends but doesn't stretch.

Things that are usually blue.Sky: The sky is blue because air scatters short blue wavelengths of sunlight more than red, a process called Rayleigh scattering.
Things that are usually blue.Blueberry: Blueberries get their blue from a waxy bloom that scatters light, as their flesh is actually pale green and the juice is purple.
Things that are usually blue.Blue jay: A blue jay's feathers have no blue pigment: their structure scatters light in a way that produces the color.
Things that are usually blue.Sapphire: Sapphires are the same mineral as rubies, corundum, and traces of iron and titanium give them their blue.
Things that are usually blue.Bluebell: Bluebells carpet British woodlands in spring, and the UK is home to about half the world's population.
Things that are usually blue.Smurf: Smurfs were created by the Belgian cartoonist Peyo in 1958, and they stand only 'three apples high'.
Things that are usually blue.Cookie Monster: Cookie Monster has been on Sesame Street since 1969, and he was later written to be more health-minded, saying cookies are a 'sometimes food'.
Things that are usually blue.Cornflower: The cornflower's bright blue gives the color its name, and it's the national flower of Estonia.
Things that are usually blue.Morpho butterfly: The morpho butterfly's wings shimmer blue from microscopic structures on its scales, not pigment, so the color shifts with angle.
Things that are usually blue.Sonic the Hedgehog: Sega's blue mascot debuted in 1991, and his color was chosen to match the company's logo.
Things that are usually blue.Dory: Dory is the forgetful blue tang in Finding Nemo, voiced by Ellen DeGeneres, and she got her own film in 2016.
Things that are usually blue.Stitch: Stitch is the blue alien from Disney's Lilo & Stitch in 2002, and he's known as Experiment 626.
Things that are usually blue.Grover: Grover is Sesame Street's furry blue monster, and he often introduces himself as 'your lovable, furry old Grover'.
Things that are usually blue.Ruby: A ruby is red, colored by chromium, and it's the same mineral as the blue sapphire.
Things that are usually blue.Emerald: An emerald is green, a variety of beryl colored by chromium and sometimes vanadium.
Things that are usually blue.Canary: Canaries are yellow, and coal miners once carried them as early warning for toxic gases.
Things that are usually blue.Cardinal: A male cardinal is bright red thanks to carotenoid pigments in its diet.
Things that are usually blue.Flamingo: Flamingos are pink from carotenoids in their diet of algae and shrimp, and chicks are born gray.
Things that are usually blue.Elmo: Elmo is a red monster on Sesame Street who refers to himself in the third person.
Things that are usually blue.Big Bird: Big Bird is yellow, stands about 8 feet 2 inches tall, and is a Sesame Street fixture.
Things that are usually blue.Kermit the Frog: Kermit is green, and the Muppet was originally made from Jim Henson's mother's old coat.
Things that are usually blue.Shrek: Shrek is a green ogre whose name comes from a Yiddish and German word for 'fright'.
Things that are usually blue.Garfield: Garfield is an orange cat who loves lasagna, and Jim Davis created the comic strip in 1978.
Things that are usually blue.Pikachu: Pikachu is the yellow electric mouse Pokemon, and its name comes from Japanese words for a spark sound and a mouse's squeak.

Things with a core.Apple: The core holds the seeds, which contain traces of amygdalin, and a person would need to eat a lot of them to be harmed.
Things with a core.Pear: A pear's core is gritty with stone cells, and the fruit ripens from the inside out, so pick it while firm.
Things with a core.Planet Earth: Earth's inner core is a solid ball of iron and nickel about as hot as the surface of the Sun.
Things with a core.Pineapple: The pineapple's core is tough and edible, and it contains the enzyme bromelain, which breaks down protein.
Things with a core.Golf ball: Modern golf balls have a rubbery core surrounded by layers, and the dimpled cover helps them fly farther.
Things with a core.Baseball: A baseball has a cork and rubber center wound with yarn, and it has exactly 108 double stitches.
Things with a core.Pencil: The core of a pencil is graphite mixed with clay, and the proportions set how hard or soft it writes.
Things with a core.Nuclear reactor: The reactor core holds the fuel rods, where fission heat boils water to drive turbines.
Things with a core.The Sun: The Sun's core reaches about 15 million degrees Celsius, where hydrogen fuses into helium.
Things with a core.Iceberg lettuce: Iceberg lettuce has a hard, dense core that's cut out with a twist, and the name came from being shipped on ice.
Things with a core.Cabbage: A cabbage's tough core sits at the base of the head, and it's edible, if chewy, and often used in broths.
Things with a core.Quince: Quince is a hard fruit related to apples and pears, and it has a core that's removed before cooking into a rosy jam.
Things with a core.Banana: Bananas have no core, only tiny seeds in wild types, and the farmed ones are sterile and seedless.
Things with a core.Grape: Grapes have no core, and the seeds are scattered through the flesh, with seedless varieties bred by humans.
Things with a core.Blueberry: Blueberries have tiny seeds spread through the flesh and no core, and their waxy bloom protects them.
Things with a core.Ping-pong ball: Ping-pong balls are hollow celluloid or plastic with no core, and weigh just 2.7 grams.
Things with a core.Balloon: A balloon is hollow rubber with just air inside, so there's no core.
Things with a core.Soap bubble: A soap bubble is a thin film of water between soap layers, and it's hollow inside.
Things with a core.Raspberry: A raspberry is made of tiny drupelets around a hollow center, so it has no core.
Things with a core.Cherry: A cherry has a single hard pit, not a core, and pits belong to the stone fruit family.
Things with a core.Watermelon: A watermelon is about 92 percent water and has seeds scattered throughout, with no core.
Things with a core.Feather: A feather has a hollow shaft called a calamus, but no core.
Things with a core.Sock: A sock is just knit fabric, with no core.
Things with a core.Pancake: A pancake is the same all the way through, with bubbles from the leavening, and no core.

Things found at a typical school.Blackboard: Schools in the early 1800s adopted blackboards, and the first in US classrooms is credited to James Pillans or others around 1801.
Things found at a typical school.Locker: School lockers became common in the 20th century, and their combination locks have long inspired students' tricks.
Things found at a typical school.Cafeteria: The word comes from Spanish for coffee shop, and self-serve cafeterias spread in the US around the 1890s.
Things found at a typical school.Gymnasium: The word comes from Greek 'gymnos' meaning naked, since ancient Greeks exercised without clothes.
Things found at a typical school.Library: The word comes from Latin 'liber', meaning book, and the earliest known school libraries were in ancient Mesopotamia.
Things found at a typical school.Desk: School desks were once bench-style for several students, with ink wells in the top, before single seats took over.
Things found at a typical school.Report card: Many early report cards were handwritten, and the first formal grading with letters was used at Mount Holyoke in 1897.
Things found at a typical school.Playground: The first playgrounds in Germany in the 1800s were sand gardens, and the modern concept spread from there to the US.
Things found at a typical school.Science lab: Many labs have eyewash stations and Bunsen burners, and the Bunsen burner is named after chemist Robert Bunsen.
Things found at a typical school.Classroom: The one-room schoolhouse was common in rural America, and some still exist where one teacher teaches every grade.
Things found at a typical school.Staff room: A teachers' hideout, famously stocked with a kettle, and often a mystery to pupils who are barred from entering.
Things found at a typical school.Cockpit: The word was first used for pits where roosters fought, and later for the pilot's area of a plane, but it's not at school.
Things found at a typical school.Runway: Airports' long strips are numbered by compass heading, so Runway 27 points west, but it has no place at school.
Things found at a typical school.Courtroom: Legal trials happen here, but only the mock trial club or a law class might bring the setting to school.
Things found at a typical school.Jail cell: A jail cell is a very far cry from school halls, and the word 'cell' comes from Latin for a small room.
Things found at a typical school.Engine room: It's the heart of a ship, where engines roar, so it won't be found at a typical school.
Things found at a typical school.Bank vault: Modern vaults can have walls of steel-reinforced concrete up to a metre thick, but schools tend to keep cash lightly.
Things found at a typical school.Stable: Where horses are kept, and while some boarding schools have riding stables, a typical school doesn't.
Things found at a typical school.Casino: Gambling halls aren't school fixtures, and the word 'casino' originally meant a small Italian villa.
Things found at a typical school.Pit lane: Race teams service cars here, with the fastest F1 pit stops taking under two seconds, but not in a typical school.
Things found at a typical school.Jury box: Where jurors sit in a courtroom, and the jury system is typically absent in a school hall.
Things found at a typical school.Hangar: Where airplanes are stored, from the French for shed, and nowhere you'd expect at school.
Things found at a typical school.Gangplank: A ship's walkway to the dock, and pirates in fiction made captives walk the plank, but not at school.
Things found at a typical school.Morgue: The word comes from a Paris building where unidentified bodies were displayed, and is no school facility.

Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Shamrock: Legend says St. Patrick used the three-leaf shamrock to explain the Trinity. It is Ireland's national emblem, worn on lapels every March 17.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Leprechaun: Leprechauns are Irish fairy cobblers in folklore. The tiny, jolly figure in green was largely invented by 20th-century American advertising.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Pot of gold: In Irish tales, a leprechaun's hidden gold lies at the rainbow's end. The pot of gold is a symbol of luck rather than any real treasure.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Green beer: Dyed green beer is mostly an American party custom. Chicago even dyes its river green each year for the holiday.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Four-leaf clover: Roughly one in 10,000 clovers has four leaves, making it a rare symbol of luck, quite distinct from the three-leaf shamrock.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Corned beef: Irish-Americans in the 1800s swapped pricey bacon for cheaper corned beef from Jewish butchers. It's now the holiday's American dish, not an Irish one.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Irish flag: The Irish tricolor has green, white and orange stripes. White stands for peace between the Catholics, in green, and Protestants, in orange.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Harp: Ireland's national emblem is the harp, found on coins and Guinness labels. It is the only country with a musical instrument as its symbol.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Shillelagh: A shillelagh is an Irish walking stick and club of blackthorn or oak. It's named after a village in County Wicklow.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Green hat: Wearing green on St. Patrick's Day is said to make you invisible to leprechauns, who pinch those who don't. Green hats are a festive staple.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Cupid: Cupid is for Valentine's Day in February, with his bow and arrows of love, not for the Irish saint's day.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Pumpkin: Pumpkins belong to autumn, for Halloween carving and Thanksgiving pie, long after March when St. Patrick's Day falls.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Tinsel: Tinsel is shimmering decoration for Christmas trees in December. March 17 is dressed in green instead.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Mistletoe: Mistletoe is a Christmas plant for December kissing, which doesn't fit a green March celebration.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Egg hunt: Egg hunts are Easter fun in spring. Easter can fall near March 17, but it is a separate celebration.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Dreidel: A dreidel is the four-sided spinning top of Hanukkah, a December festival of lights, nowhere near the Irish celebration.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Candy cane: Candy canes are Christmas sweets that hang on trees in December. March 17's treats are more likely soda bread and green beer.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Turkey: Turkey is the main dish at American Thanksgiving in November. St. Patrick's Day food leans toward corned beef and cabbage.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Piñata: The piñata is a papier-mâché figure packed with candy, smashed at Mexican parties. It's not an Irish symbol at all.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Maple leaf: The maple leaf is Canada's national symbol, found on its flag. Ireland's equivalent is the shamrock or the harp.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Thistle: The thistle is Scotland's national flower. It could trick you since Scotland is Celtic like Ireland, but it's a different country.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Red rose: The red rose stands for England and for Valentine's romance. Ireland's plant symbol is the shamrock, not a rose.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Lantern: Lanterns light the Chinese Lantern Festival and mid-autumn celebrations, not an Irish saint's day in March.
Symbols of St. Patrick's Day.Tulip: The tulip is the Netherlands' famous spring flower, long tied to Dutch trade, not to Ireland's holiday.

Santa's reindeer.Dasher: First of the eight named in the 1823 poem "A Visit from St. Nicholas," where he leads the team as the sleigh sweeps off.
Santa's reindeer.Dancer: One of the original eight from the 1823 poem; the name hints at the nimble footwork needed to land on steep rooftops.
Santa's reindeer.Prancer: To prance is to spring with high, showy steps, like a parade horse, which makes the name a good fit for a flying team.
Santa's reindeer.Vixen: Also the word for a female fox, which makes this one of the few reindeer names borrowed from a different animal.
Santa's reindeer.Comet: Named for the streaking object in the night sky; in the 1823 poem he is called out right after Dasher, Dancer, Prancer and Vixen.
Santa's reindeer.Cupid: Named for the Roman god of love, the only name on the team drawn from classical mythology.
Santa's reindeer.Donner: German for thunder. In the 1823 poem he was actually called Dunder, and his partner Blixem, before both were reworked.
Santa's reindeer.Blitzen: German for lightning. The original 1823 poem called him Blixem, and the name was changed to Blitzen in later editions.
Santa's reindeer.Rudolph: The ninth reindeer was invented in 1939 by Robert L. May for a Montgomery Ward giveaway booklet, and millions were handed out.
Santa's reindeer.Sven: Kristoff's loyal reindeer in Disney's Frozen. Sven never speaks; Kristoff does his voice, with a goofy, higher tone.
Santa's reindeer.Bambi: A fawn, not a reindeer. In Felix Salten's 1923 novel, Bambi is a roe deer; Disney's 1942 film made him a white-tailed deer.
Santa's reindeer.Thumper: Bambi's rabbit friend, not a deer. His name comes from his habit of thumping a hind foot, which real rabbits do as an alarm.
Santa's reindeer.Dumbo: A baby elephant with enormous ears, from Disney's 1941 film, which runs only about an hour and is one of its shortest features.
Santa's reindeer.Frosty: A snowman, not a reindeer. His song arrived in 1950, a year after Gene Autry's hit about Rudolph.
Santa's reindeer.Jingles: Sounds festive, but it isn't a reindeer. The song "Jingle Bells" was published in 1857 under the title "One Horse Open Sleigh."
Santa's reindeer.Twinkle: Cute, but no reindeer has it. The nursery tune for "Twinkle, Twinkle" is borrowed from a French melody, "Ah! vous dirai-je, maman."
Santa's reindeer.Buddy: The human raised among elves in the 2003 movie Elf. Played by Will Ferrell, he is far too big for every elf-sized door.
Santa's reindeer.Grinch: Dr. Seuss's green grump from the 1957 book, who steals Christmas. His heart famously grows three sizes at the end.
Santa's reindeer.Max: The Grinch's dog, who is forced to wear a fake antler and play reindeer to pull the stolen-presents sleigh.
Santa's reindeer.Hermey: The elf who dreams of being a dentist in the 1964 TV special Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer. He is a misfit, not a reindeer.
Santa's reindeer.Snowball: A common pet name, and the pig in Orwell's Animal Farm who is driven out by Napoleon. Not on Santa's team.
Santa's reindeer.Pegasus: A winged horse of Greek myth that sprang from Medusa's blood. He flies like a reindeer, but pulls no sleighs.
Santa's reindeer.Hedwig: Harry Potter's snowy owl, a birthday gift from Hagrid. Her name came from a saint he spotted in a history book.
Santa's reindeer.Bolt: The Disney dog who believes his TV superpowers are real. Not a reindeer, though he is good at running fast.

Famous dolls and action figures.Barbie: Her full name is Barbara Millicent Roberts, and she debuted in 1959.
Famous dolls and action figures.Ken: Named after Ruth Handler's son Kenneth, and introduced in 1961 as Barbie's boyfriend.
Famous dolls and action figures.G.I. Joe: Hasbro called him an action figure in 1964 so boys would not feel like they were playing with dolls.
Famous dolls and action figures.Cabbage Patch Kids: Each came with a birth certificate and adoption papers, and the 1983 craze led shoppers to brawl in stores.
Famous dolls and action figures.American Girl: Launched in 1986, each doll comes with a story set in a particular moment of history.
Famous dolls and action figures.Bratz: Launched in 2001 with big heads and bold fashion, and it fought a long legal battle with Mattel.
Famous dolls and action figures.Polly Pocket: Tiny dolls that fit inside a compact, created in 1983 by Chris Wiggs for his daughter.
Famous dolls and action figures.Raggedy Ann: Created by Johnny Gruelle in 1915; the name blends two James Whitcomb Riley poems, The Raggedy Man and Little Orphant Annie.
Famous dolls and action figures.Action Man: Britain's version of G.I. Joe, launched by Palitoy in 1966.
Famous dolls and action figures.Sindy: Britain's best-selling doll for decades after 1963, and Barbie's main rival there.
Famous dolls and action figures.Kewpie: Created in 1909 by Rose O'Neill, based on Cupid, and first drawn in comic strips.
Famous dolls and action figures.Furby: A fuzzy electronic pet, not a doll or action figure.
Famous dolls and action figures.Tamagotchi: A virtual pet; the name comes from Japanese tamago, egg, plus watch.
Famous dolls and action figures.Slinky: A steel coil spring, famed for walking down stairs, but not a doll or figure.
Famous dolls and action figures.Etch A Sketch: A drawing toy, and the gray lines come from aluminum powder behind the screen.
Famous dolls and action figures.Lite-Brite: A 1967 Hasbro toy where colored pegs light up to make glowing pictures.
Famous dolls and action figures.Spirograph: A drawing toy invented in 1965 by British engineer Denys Fisher.
Famous dolls and action figures.Play-Doh: Originally invented as a wallpaper cleaner before it became a toy.
Famous dolls and action figures.Lego: The name comes from Danish leg godt, play well.
Famous dolls and action figures.Rubik's Cube: Has 43 quintillion possible positions, but it is a puzzle, not a doll.
Famous dolls and action figures.Hot Wheels: Mattel launched these toy cars in 1968 to rival Matchbox.
Famous dolls and action figures.Nerf: A foam ball first sold in 1970; the name may come from non-expanding recreational foam.
Famous dolls and action figures.Magic 8-Ball: Gives one of 20 answers, ten positive, five unsure and five negative; it is a fortune toy, not a doll.
Famous dolls and action figures.Monopoly: A board game, with mascot Mr. Monopoly (Rich Uncle Pennybags), but not a doll.

Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Dasher: The first reindeer named in the 1823 poem A Visit from St. Nicholas, which listed eight in all.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Dancer: One of the original eight reindeer in Clement Clarke Moore's poem, a name that evokes graceful leaps.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Prancer: Named in the 1823 poem, and a favourite of the famous song's lyrics, whose name suggests high-stepping.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Vixen: Originally a female fox's name, it is a name in Santa's team, which appears in the poem as Vixen.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Comet: Named in the 1823 poem, among the reindeer who fly through the night sky.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Cupid: The reindeer shares his name with the Roman god of love.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Donner: This name is German for thunder, and originally in the poem it was Dunder, later changed to Donder and Donner.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Blitzen: The German word for lightning, which pairs with Donner, thunder; in the original poem he was Blixem.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Rudolph: Created in 1939 by Robert L. May for Montgomery Ward, and made famous by a 1949 song that Gene Autry recorded.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Sven: Sven is Kristoff's loyal reindeer from Disney's Frozen, voiced by grunts, so he's not part of Santa's team.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Bambi: Bambi is a young deer from Felix Salten's 1923 novel and Disney's 1942 film, a white-tailed deer and not on Santa's sleigh.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Faline: Faline is Bambi's mate in Felix Salten's story and Disney's film, so she is a forest deer, not a sleigh reindeer.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Dazzler: Dazzler sounds plausible, but it's a Marvel mutant who fights with light, and no reindeer by that name is in the poem.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Flasher: It sounds festive and speedy like Comet, but the poem's eight names are Dasher, Dancer, Prancer, Vixen, Comet, Cupid, Donner and Blitzen.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Twinkle: It's a plausible-sounding invention, but Clement Moore's 1823 poem lists exactly eight reindeer, and none is Twinkle.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Sprinter: It echoes Dasher's speed, but the poem's team has no Sprinter; only eight names are traditional, plus Rudolph.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Blazer: Blazer sounds like a fiery reindeer, but it's no part of the traditional list that Moore's poem gave.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Nimbus: Nimbus is a cloud type, and in Harry Potter a racing broom, the Nimbus 2000; no reindeer carries the name.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Stomper: It may fit a heavy-footed deer, yet the classic roster has no Stomper; the poem's eight are all named in lines.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Bounder: Bounder is an old British word for a rascal; it sounds like a leaping reindeer but isn't one on the team.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Sparkle: It's a fitting festive word, but none of Santa's traditional reindeer, in poem or song, bears it.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Scooter: Scooter sounds cheerful, but the famous team of nine, with Rudolph, has no reindeer of that name.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Glider: Glider sounds like a fitting flier, but the poem's list doesn't include it; Dasher and Dancer are far older names.
Santa's sleigh team (Rudolph included).Hopper: Reindeer are runners, not hoppers, and Hopper isn't among the nine in Moore's poem or the Rudolph song.

Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Mayflower: The ship carried 102 passengers in 1620 and had previously hauled cargo such as wine.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Plymouth: The colony took its name from the English port the Pilgrims last sailed from.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Pilgrims: Mostly English Separatists who sought religious freedom; many first spent years in the Netherlands.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Wampanoag: Their name means 'People of the First Light', and they lived in the region for thousands of years before the Pilgrims came.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Squanto: He spoke English because he had been captured and taken to Europe years before, and he taught the Pilgrims to plant corn with fish.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Massasoit: The Wampanoag sachem who made a peace treaty with the Pilgrims in 1621 that held for about 50 years.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.William Bradford: He governed Plymouth Colony for most of three decades and wrote Of Plymouth Plantation, our best source on the settlement.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Myles Standish: The colony's hired military leader was a professional soldier, not a member of the Separatist church.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Cape Cod: The Pilgrims first landed here in November 1620, then moved on to settle at Plymouth.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Plymouth Rock: Its link to the Pilgrims was first claimed over 120 years later, and the rock has been moved and chipped away.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Governor Carver: John Carver was Plymouth's first governor and died in spring 1621, just months after the landing.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Jamestown: Founded in 1607 in Virginia, 13 years before Plymouth, so a different colony entirely.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Pocahontas: Daughter of Chief Powhatan and tied to Jamestown, not Plymouth.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.John Smith: Jamestown's leader, but he did map the New England coast in 1614 and gave the region its name.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Roanoke: The Lost Colony vanished in the 1580s, decades before the Mayflower.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Santa Maria: Columbus's 1492 flagship ran aground off Hispaniola that Christmas Day, long before the Pilgrims.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Columbus: He died in 1506, over a century before the Mayflower sailed.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Salem: The 1692 witch trials happened here in a Puritan colony, but they are no part of the first Thanksgiving.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Powhatan: Chief of the Powhatan Confederacy in Virginia, far from Plymouth.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Sacagawea: Guided Lewis and Clark in 1805, nearly two centuries after the Pilgrims.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Lewis and Clark: Explored westward from 1804, almost two centuries after the Mayflower.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Paul Revere: His 1775 ride came 155 years after the Mayflower landed.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Susan Constant: The largest of the three ships that reached Jamestown in 1607.
Plymouth and the first Thanksgiving.Godspeed: One of the three Jamestown ships of 1607; the Mayflower came 13 years later.
